Deuteronomy 1.summary: Moses begins his farewell addresses on the plains of Moab, in the eleventh month of the fortieth year after the exodus (Deuteronomy 1:1-5). He first looks back: the LORD told Israel to leave Horeb and take the land promised to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob (Deuteronomy 1:6-8). Moses recalls appointing wise leaders and judges to share the burden of governing and charging them to judge fairly (Deuteronomy 1:9-18). He then retells the failure at Kadesh-barnea: twelve men scouted the land and brought back a good report, yet the people refused to go up out of fear (Deuteronomy 1:19-33). As a result that generation was barred from entering, except Caleb, and Moses himself was told he would not enter (Deuteronomy 1:34-38). The people then attacked without God's presence and were driven back (Deuteronomy 1:41-46). The chapter sets up the whole book: remember what happened, and trust God this time.
Deuteronomy 1.whereWeAre: Numbers ended with Israel camped on the plains of Moab, ready to cross the Jordan. Deuteronomy records Moses' farewell speeches to the new generation there, in the last weeks of his life. He starts by retelling the spies' failure from Numbers 13–14, and his history lesson continues through chapter 3.

Deuteronomy 2.summary: Moses continues recalling the wilderness years. After a long time circling Mount Seir, Israel is told to turn north and to treat Edom (the descendants of Esau), Moab, and Ammon with restraint, because the LORD had given those lands to them (Deuteronomy 2:1-9; Deuteronomy 2:17-19). Israel buys food and water along the way (Deuteronomy 2:6; Deuteronomy 2:28-29). Thirty-eight years passed from Kadesh-barnea until the whole generation of fighting men had died, "as the LORD sware unto them" (Deuteronomy 2:14-15). Israel then crosses the Arnon Valley, where Sihon king of Heshbon refuses passage; the LORD hardens his spirit, and Israel defeats him and takes his cities (Deuteronomy 2:24-37). The chapter shows God directing both Israel's patience and its victories.
Deuteronomy 2.whereWeAre: Moses' retelling in chapter 1 ended with Israel's defeat after refusing to enter the land. Now he covers the thirty-eight years of wandering that followed and the turn north past Edom, Moab, and Ammon. The first victory, over Sihon, leads into the defeat of Og in chapter 3.

Deuteronomy 3.summary: Moses recalls Israel's defeat of Og king of Bashan, whose sixty fortified cities were taken (Deuteronomy 3:1-11). He then describes how the land east of the Jordan was given to Reuben, Gad, and half the tribe of Manasseh, on the condition that their fighting men cross over armed to help the other tribes (Deuteronomy 3:12-20). Joshua is reminded that the LORD will fight for Israel (Deuteronomy 3:21-22). Moses then tells how he pleaded to see the land, but the LORD said, "Let it suffice thee; speak no more unto me of this matter," and allowed him only to view it from Pisgah (Deuteronomy 3:23-27). He is told to commission and encourage Joshua, who will lead the people (Deuteronomy 3:28).
Deuteronomy 3.whereWeAre: Chapter 2 ended with Israel's victory over Sihon. Moses now recalls the defeat of Og, how the land east of the Jordan was given to two and a half tribes, and his own plea to enter the land. This finishes his history lesson, and in chapter 4 he turns to what it means for Israel now.

Deuteronomy 4.summary: Moses urges Israel to obey the laws and rules he is about to teach, and not to add to or subtract from them, since obedience will show the nations Israel's wisdom (Deuteronomy 4:1-8). He reminds them that at Horeb they heard the LORD's voice from the fire but saw no form, so they must not make idols (Deuteronomy 4:9-24). He warns that if they fall into idolatry they will be scattered among the nations, but also promises that if they seek the LORD with all their heart they will find him, because he is merciful and will not forget his covenant (Deuteronomy 4:25-31). Moses marvels at the uniqueness of what God has done and of the LORD alone being God (Deuteronomy 4:32-40). He sets apart three cities of refuge east of the Jordan (Deuteronomy 4:41-43) and introduces the law he will set before them (Deuteronomy 4:44-49).
Deuteronomy 4.whereWeAre: Moses has spent chapters 1–3 retelling the journey from Sinai to here. Now he draws the lesson: obey God and never worship idols, because at Sinai Israel heard God's voice but saw no shape. This ends Moses' first speech; his second, the heart of the book, begins in chapter 5.

Deuteronomy 5.summary: Moses gathers all Israel and repeats the Ten Commandments, reminding them that the LORD made this covenant not only with their ancestors but with the people standing before him (Deuteronomy 5:1-5). The commandments address exclusive loyalty to the LORD, no idols, the proper use of God's name, Sabbath rest, honoring parents, and prohibitions on murder, adultery, theft, false witness, and coveting (Deuteronomy 5:6-21). The Sabbath is tied here to remembering the slavery in Egypt (Deuteronomy 5:12-15). The people had been terrified by the fire and voice at Horeb and asked Moses to be their go-between; the LORD approved and wished that they would always fear him and keep his commands (Deuteronomy 5:22-31). Moses closes by urging them to walk exactly in the way commanded (Deuteronomy 5:32-33).
Deuteronomy 5.whereWeAre: Moses' first speech ended in chapter 4. His second speech begins by repeating the Ten Commandments, first given at Sinai in Exodus 20, to the new generation. Chapters 6–11 explain the heart behind these commands, and chapters 12–26 apply them in detail.

Deuteronomy 6.summary: This chapter contains the famous Shema: "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD: And thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thine heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might" (Deuteronomy 6:4-5). Moses instructs Israel to keep these words on their hearts, teach them diligently to their children, talk about them throughout the day, and bind and write them as visible reminders (Deuteronomy 6:6-9). He warns that when they enjoy houses they did not build and vineyards they did not plant, they must not forget the LORD who brought them out of Egypt (Deuteronomy 6:10-15), nor test him as at Massah (Deuteronomy 6:16). When children ask about the meaning of the laws, parents are to retell the story of the exodus (Deuteronomy 6:20-25).
Deuteronomy 6.whereWeAre: Moses has just repeated the Ten Commandments in chapter 5. Here he gives their heart: "Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD" (Deuteronomy 6:4). Jesus calls the next verse the first and great commandment (Matthew 22:37–38), and chapters 7–11 keep explaining what this love looks like.

Deuteronomy 7.summary: As Israel prepares to enter Canaan, Moses commands them to drive out seven nations and make no covenant or intermarriage with them, for fear they will turn Israel away from the LORD; their altars and sacred objects are to be torn down (Deuteronomy 7:1-6). Israel is a holy people chosen not because it was large or special, but because the LORD loved them and kept his oath (Deuteronomy 7:7-8). God is faithful to those who love him and keep his commands, to a thousand generations (Deuteronomy 7:9-11). Obedience will bring blessing and health (Deuteronomy 7:12-16). Israel is told not to fear nations that seem stronger, since the LORD will drive them out gradually (Deuteronomy 7:17-24), and not to covet or keep the idols' gold and silver (Deuteronomy 7:25-26).
Deuteronomy 7.whereWeAre: Chapter 6 called Israel to love the LORD with all their heart. Now Moses applies that to the nations living in Canaan: Israel must not take up their gods. He reminds them that God chose them out of love, not because they were great, and chapter 8 warns about forgetting God when life gets easy.

Deuteronomy 8.summary: Moses calls Israel to remember the forty years in the wilderness, when God humbled and tested them, letting them hunger and then feeding them with manna so they would learn that "man doth not live by bread only, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of the LORD doth man live" (Deuteronomy 8:1-3). Their clothes did not wear out, and God disciplined them as a father (Deuteronomy 8:4-5). The land ahead is described as good, with water, grain, vines, figs, pomegranates, olive oil, honey, iron, and copper (Deuteronomy 8:7-10). Moses warns that when they are full and prosperous, they must not forget the LORD or say "My power and the might of mine hand hath gotten me this wealth" (Deuteronomy 8:11-18). Forgetting God and following other gods will lead to destruction (Deuteronomy 8:19-20).
Deuteronomy 8.whereWeAre: Chapter 7 warned Israel about the nations' gods. Now Moses warns about a quieter danger: forgetting God once they are rich and comfortable. He looks back on the forty years of manna, and chapter 9 reminds them that they do not deserve the land.

Deuteronomy 9.summary: Moses tells Israel that as they cross the Jordan to face larger and stronger nations, including the Anakim, they must not think the LORD gives them the land because of their righteousness (Deuteronomy 9:1-6). It is because of the wickedness of those nations and because of the oath to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Israel is called "a stiffnecked people." Moses then recounts their rebellions, especially the golden calf at Horeb: he was on the mountain forty days when the people made the calf; the LORD was ready to destroy them; Moses broke the tablets, interceded for forty days, and destroyed the calf (Deuteronomy 9:7-21). He mentions other rebellions at Taberah, Massah, Kibroth-hattaavah, and Kadesh-barnea (Deuteronomy 9:22-24) and recalls his prayer asking God to remember his servants and his own people (Deuteronomy 9:25-29).
Deuteronomy 9.whereWeAre: Chapter 8 warned against pride in wealth. This chapter warns against pride in being good, for Moses tells them, "thou art a stiffnecked people" (Deuteronomy 9:6). To prove it, he retells the golden calf, a story that continues into chapter 10.

Deuteronomy 10.summary: Moses continues the golden calf story: the LORD told him to cut two new tablets and make an ark of acacia wood to hold them, which he did (Deuteronomy 10:1-5). A brief travel note follows, including the death of Aaron, the succession of his son Eleazar as priest, and the setting apart of the tribe of Levi to carry the ark, serve, and bless in God's name; Levi has no land inheritance because the LORD is their inheritance (Deuteronomy 10:6-9). The LORD again listens to Moses and tells him to lead the people on (Deuteronomy 10:10-11). Then comes a central summary of what God asks: fear him, walk in his ways, love him, serve him with all one's heart and soul, and keep his commands (Deuteronomy 10:12-13). God is Lord of lords who loves the stranger, and Israel must too, remembering that they were strangers in Egypt (Deuteronomy 10:17-19). Moses reminds them that seventy people went down to Egypt and God has made them like the stars (Deuteronomy 10:22).
Deuteronomy 10.whereWeAre: Moses' retelling of the golden calf from chapter 9 ends here with the new stone tablets. Then he sums up what God wants: "to fear the LORD thy God, to walk in all his ways, and to love him" (Deuteronomy 10:12). Chapter 11 closes this part of Moses' speech.

Deuteronomy 11.summary: Moses urges Israel to love the LORD and keep his commands. He reminds the people, especially those who witnessed it, of what the LORD did in Egypt, in the wilderness, and to Dathan and Abiram, when the earth swallowed them (Deuteronomy 11:1-7). The land they are entering is not like Egypt, where crops were watered by human effort, but is a land of hills and valleys that drinks rain from heaven and is cared for by the LORD (Deuteronomy 11:8-12). Obedience will bring rain in its season; turning to other gods will bring drought (Deuteronomy 11:13-17). Israel is to place these words on their hearts, teach them to their children, and write them on doorposts (Deuteronomy 11:18-21). Moses then sets before them blessing and curse and instructs them to proclaim the blessing on Mount Gerizim and the curse on Mount Ebal (Deuteronomy 11:26-32).
Deuteronomy 11.whereWeAre: This chapter closes the part of Moses' speech that began in chapter 5. He reminds Israel of what they have seen God do and sets before them a blessing and a curse. Starting in chapter 12, he turns to the specific laws for life in the land.

Deuteronomy 12.summary: Moses begins the specific laws by commanding Israel to destroy the places where the nations worshiped their gods and to worship the LORD only at "the place which the LORD your God shall choose" (Deuteronomy 12:1-14). There they are to bring offerings, tithes, and firstfruits and rejoice before the LORD with their households and the Levites. Eating meat at home is permitted, though blood must not be eaten because it represents life (Deuteronomy 12:15-28). Israel is warned not to ask how the nations served their gods and then do the same, since those nations even burned their sons and daughters to their gods (Deuteronomy 12:29-31). The chapter ends with the instruction to do all that is commanded without adding or taking away (Deuteronomy 12:32).
Deuteronomy 12.whereWeAre: Chapters 5–11 explained the heart of the covenant: love God and keep his commands. Now chapters 12–26 give the specific laws, starting with worship. Israel must tear down the Canaanites' shrines and worship at the one place God chooses, and chapter 13 deals with anyone who leads people to other gods.

Deuteronomy 13.summary: Three scenarios test Israel's loyalty to the LORD alone. First, a prophet or dreamer who gives a sign and then urges following other gods is to be rejected, because the LORD is testing whether Israel loves him with all its heart (Deuteronomy 13:1-5). Second, a close relative or friend who secretly entices someone to worship other gods must not be spared or concealed, and the matter must be exposed (Deuteronomy 13:6-11). Third, if a whole town is reported to have been led astray, Israel must investigate carefully, and if the report is true, the town is to be devoted to destruction (Deuteronomy 13:12-18). In each case the stated purpose is to remove evil from among them and to preserve fear of the LORD.
Deuteronomy 13.whereWeAre: Chapter 12 told Israel where and how to worship the LORD. This chapter protects that worship from the inside, whether the pull toward other gods comes from a prophet, a family member, or a whole town. Chapter 14 turns to the everyday marks of being God's holy people.

Deuteronomy 14.summary: Israel, as children of the LORD, are told not to cut themselves or shave their foreheads for the dead (Deuteronomy 14:1-2). The chapter then lists animals that may and may not be eaten, including land animals, water creatures, birds, and insects, and prohibits eating anything that died on its own or boiling a young goat in its mother's milk (Deuteronomy 14:3-21). Finally, Israel is to set aside a tithe of grain, wine, and oil each year and eat it joyfully before the LORD at the chosen place; if the journey is too long, the produce may be exchanged for silver (Deuteronomy 14:22-27). Every third year the tithe is to be stored in the towns for the Levites, the foreigner, the fatherless, and the widow (Deuteronomy 14:28-29).
Deuteronomy 14.whereWeAre: Chapter 13 dealt with the danger of other gods. This chapter covers everyday marks of belonging to God: how to mourn, what to eat, and how to give a tenth of the harvest. Chapter 15 continues with care for the poor.

Deuteronomy 15.summary: Every seventh year, Israelites are to release debts owed by fellow Israelites (Deuteronomy 15:1-6). Moses says there should be no poor among them if they obey, yet also acknowledges the poor will not cease from the land, so they must open their hands generously and not harden their hearts, even when the seventh year is near (Deuteronomy 15:4; Deuteronomy 15:7-11). Hebrew slaves, male or female, are to be released in the seventh year and sent away with generous provision, remembering that Israel was once a slave in Egypt (Deuteronomy 15:12-15). A servant who loves his master and wishes to stay may have his ear pierced with an awl as a permanent servant (Deuteronomy 15:16-17). Firstborn male animals are to be consecrated to the LORD and eaten at the chosen place, unless blemished (Deuteronomy 15:19-23).
Deuteronomy 15.whereWeAre: The tithe for the poor at the end of chapter 14 leads into this chapter on generosity. Every seventh year debts are cancelled, and Hebrew servants go free. Chapter 16 turns to Israel's three yearly feasts.

Deuteronomy 16.summary: Moses lays out three pilgrim festivals. Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread commemorate the exodus from Egypt and are to be observed at the chosen place (Deuteronomy 16:1-8). The Feast of Weeks comes seven weeks after the grain harvest begins, with a freewill offering and joyful celebration including servants, Levites, foreigners, orphans, and widows (Deuteronomy 16:9-12). The Feast of Booths follows the harvest of threshing floor and winepress, again with rejoicing (Deuteronomy 16:13-15). All males are to appear before the LORD at these three times, each giving as blessed (Deuteronomy 16:16-17). The chapter then turns to appointing judges and officers who must judge fairly, refuse bribes, and follow "that which is altogether just" (Deuteronomy 16:18-20), and prohibits setting up an Asherah or sacred pillar (Deuteronomy 16:21-22).
Deuteronomy 16.whereWeAre: Chapter 15 covered the seventh year of release. Now Moses sets out the three yearly feasts when Israel gathers at God's chosen place, then turns to the judges who will lead the people. That leads into chapters 17–18 on Israel's leaders.

Deuteronomy 17.summary: The chapter begins by prohibiting sacrifice of blemished animals (Deuteronomy 17:1). It then provides procedures for dealing with idolatry: a charge must be carefully investigated, and conviction requires the testimony of at least two or three witnesses, who throw the first stones (Deuteronomy 17:2-7). Difficult legal cases are to be taken to the Levitical priests and the judge at the chosen place, whose decisions are to be followed (Deuteronomy 17:8-13). Finally, if Israel later asks for a king "like as all the nations" around them, he must be chosen by the LORD, be an Israelite, not multiply horses, wives, or silver and gold, and write for himself a copy of the law to read all his life so that he does not consider himself above his brothers (Deuteronomy 17:14-20).
Deuteronomy 17.whereWeAre: Chapter 16 ended with the call to appoint fair judges. This chapter continues with the courts and then looks ahead to a day when Israel will want a king. Chapter 18 covers the priests and the prophets.

Deuteronomy 18.summary: The Levitical priests have no land inheritance and are to live on a portion of the sacrifices and firstfruits; any Levite who comes to serve at the chosen place may share in this service (Deuteronomy 18:1-8). Israel must not imitate the nations' practices, including child sacrifice, divination, sorcery, interpreting omens, and consulting mediums or the dead; these are detestable to the LORD (Deuteronomy 18:9-14). Instead, because the people were afraid to hear God's voice at Horeb, the LORD promises to raise up for them "a Prophet from the midst of thee, of thy brethren, like unto me", and to put his words in his mouth (Deuteronomy 18:15-19). A prophet who speaks presumptuously or in the name of other gods must die; if what a prophet says does not come to pass, he has not spoken from the LORD (Deuteronomy 18:20-22).
Deuteronomy 18.whereWeAre: Chapter 17 covered judges and kings. This chapter covers Israel's other leaders: the priests and Levites, and the prophets. God promises "a Prophet from the midst of thee, of thy brethren, like unto me" (Deuteronomy 18:15), a promise later applied to Jesus (Acts 3:22), and chapter 19 returns to justice.

Deuteronomy 19.summary: Once Israel settles the land, three cities of refuge are to be set apart in the middle of the land, with roads prepared, so a person who kills another unintentionally can flee there and be safe from the avenger of blood (Deuteronomy 19:1-7). If the land expands, three more are to be added (Deuteronomy 19:8-10). A murderer who flees to such a city to escape justice, however, is to be handed over (Deuteronomy 19:11-13). Boundary markers must not be moved (Deuteronomy 19:14). A single witness is insufficient to convict; two or three are required, and a malicious witness is to receive the punishment he intended for the accused, reflecting "life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth" (Deuteronomy 19:15-21).
Deuteronomy 19.whereWeAre: Chapters 16–18 covered Israel's leaders. Now Moses turns to protecting life: cities of refuge for someone who kills by accident, and strict rules against false witnesses. Chapter 20 gives rules for war.

Deuteronomy 20.summary: Moses gives rules for going to war. When Israel faces a larger army, they are not to be afraid because the LORD goes with them; a priest is to address the troops before battle (Deuteronomy 20:1-4). Officers then exempt those who have built a house but not dedicated it, planted a vineyard but not eaten from it, are engaged but not married, or are afraid and fainthearted (Deuteronomy 20:5-9). Before attacking a distant city, Israel must offer terms of peace; if the city surrenders, its people become forced laborers, and if not, the men are to be killed and others may be taken as plunder (Deuteronomy 20:10-15). Cities within the land that Israel is to inherit are to be devoted to destruction so that Israel is not taught the nations' detestable practices (Deuteronomy 20:16-18). Fruit trees must not be cut down during a siege (Deuteronomy 20:19-20).
Deuteronomy 20.whereWeAre: Chapter 19 covered justice inside Israel. This chapter gives rules for going to war, since Israel is about to fight for the land. Chapter 21 returns to life in the towns.

Deuteronomy 21.summary: Moses gives a series of laws about community responsibility. If a slain body is found in open country and the killer is unknown, the elders and judges of the nearest town measure the distance, and the town's elders break a heifer's neck in an unplowed valley with running water, wash their hands, and declare their innocence, asking the LORD for forgiveness (Deuteronomy 21:1-9). A man who wants to marry a captive woman must allow her a month to mourn her family and may not sell her if he later dismisses her (Deuteronomy 21:10-14). A firstborn son's inheritance rights cannot be shifted to a favored wife's son (Deuteronomy 21:15-17). A stubborn and rebellious son who refuses correction is brought by his parents to the elders for judgment (Deuteronomy 21:18-21). A body hung on a tree must be buried the same day, because "he that is hanged is accursed of God" and the land must not be defiled (Deuteronomy 21:22-23).
Deuteronomy 21.whereWeAre: The rules for war in chapter 20 lead into a mix of laws for town life, starting with an unsolved murder. Chapters 21–25 cover family, neighbors, and fairness in everyday situations.

Deuteronomy 22.summary: The chapter collects laws about everyday responsibility and personal relationships. Israelites must return lost animals and belongings to their owners and help a fallen animal (Deuteronomy 22:1-4). Cross-dressing is prohibited (Deuteronomy 22:5); a mother bird must not be taken with her young (Deuteronomy 22:6-7); a parapet is required on a new roof to prevent falls (Deuteronomy 22:8); mixed seed, mixed plowing, and mixed fabrics are forbidden (Deuteronomy 22:9-11), and tassels are to be worn on cloak corners (Deuteronomy 22:12). The rest of the chapter addresses marriage and sexual conduct, including a husband's false accusation of his bride's virginity (Deuteronomy 22:13-21), adultery (Deuteronomy 22:22), sexual offenses involving betrothed or unbetrothed women (Deuteronomy 22:23-29), and a man's father's wife (Deuteronomy 22:30).
Deuteronomy 22.whereWeAre: The everyday laws that began in chapter 21 continue. This chapter covers caring for a neighbor's property, small acts of kindness, and sexual purity in marriage. The laws continue in chapter 23.

Deuteronomy 23.summary: Moses lists who may not enter "the congregation of the LORD": men with certain injuries, a person of unlawful birth, and Ammonites and Moabites, who are shut out because of how they treated Israel on its journey (Deuteronomy 23:1-6); Edomites and Egyptians are not to be despised and may enter in the third generation (Deuteronomy 23:7-8). The war camp must be kept clean, with sanitary provisions, because the LORD walks in the camp (Deuteronomy 23:9-14). Escaped slaves must not be returned (Deuteronomy 23:15-16). Shrine prostitution is forbidden (Deuteronomy 23:17-18). Israelites must not charge interest to fellow Israelites, though they may charge foreigners (Deuteronomy 23:19-20). Vows must be kept (Deuteronomy 23:21-23). A traveler may eat grapes or grain from a neighbor's field but not carry any away (Deuteronomy 23:24-25).
Deuteronomy 23.whereWeAre: The everyday laws of chapters 21–22 continue. This chapter covers who may join Israel's worship, keeping the war camp clean, and fairness in lending and vows. Chapter 24 continues with laws that protect the weak.

Deuteronomy 24.summary: A mix of laws protecting people in vulnerable positions. A man who divorces his wife with a written certificate may not remarry her if she has since married and been divorced or widowed by another man (Deuteronomy 24:1-4). A newly married man is exempt from military service for a year (Deuteronomy 24:5). A millstone may not be taken as a pledge, since it is the means of daily bread (Deuteronomy 24:6); kidnapping an Israelite is a capital offense (Deuteronomy 24:7); and skin disease is to be handled as the priests direct, remembering what happened to Miriam (Deuteronomy 24:8-9). Creditors may not enter a debtor's house to take a pledge, and a poor man's cloak must be returned by sunset (Deuteronomy 24:10-13). Hired workers must be paid the same day (Deuteronomy 24:14-15). Each person is responsible for his own sin (Deuteronomy 24:16). Justice must not be denied to the foreigner, orphan, or widow, and harvest leftovers are to be left for them, remembering that Israel was a slave in Egypt (Deuteronomy 24:17-22).
Deuteronomy 24.whereWeAre: The everyday laws continue from chapter 23. This chapter protects those with little power: wives, debtors, workers, strangers, orphans, and widows. Chapter 25 brings this section of laws to a close.

Deuteronomy 25.summary: The chapter opens with limits on corporal punishment: a guilty person may be beaten by a judge in his presence, but no more than forty stripes, so that he is not degraded (Deuteronomy 25:1-3). An ox treading grain must not be muzzled (Deuteronomy 25:4). If brothers live together and one dies without a son, the surviving brother is to marry the widow so the dead man's name will not be blotted out; if he refuses, the widow publicly removes his sandal and spits in his face (Deuteronomy 25:5-10). A woman who grabs a man's private parts during a fight is to be punished (Deuteronomy 25:11-12). Honest weights and measures are required (Deuteronomy 25:13-16). The chapter ends with a command to remember what Amalek did to Israel on the way from Egypt, attacking the weary and straggling, and to blot out the memory of Amalek once Israel has rest (Deuteronomy 25:17-19).
Deuteronomy 25.whereWeAre: This chapter finishes the everyday laws of chapters 21–25. It covers fair punishment, a brother's duty to his dead brother's widow, and honest weights. It ends by remembering Amalek, and chapter 26 closes the laws that began in chapter 12.

Deuteronomy 26.summary: When Israel enters and settles the land, each worshiper is to bring the firstfruits of the harvest in a basket to the chosen place, give it to the priest, and recite a confession of faith: "A Syrian ready to perish was my father," retelling how the LORD brought them out of Egypt and gave them the land (Deuteronomy 26:1-11). Every third year, after setting aside the tithe for the Levite, foreigner, fatherless, and widow, the worshiper declares before the LORD that he has obeyed and asks for blessing (Deuteronomy 26:12-15). The chapter concludes with a mutual declaration: Israel affirms that the LORD is their God and they will keep his commands, and the LORD affirms that Israel is his treasured people, set high above all nations in praise and honor (Deuteronomy 26:16-19).
Deuteronomy 26.whereWeAre: The laws that began in chapter 12 close here. Moses tells Israel what to say when they bring their first harvest in the land: "A Syrian ready to perish was my father" (Deuteronomy 26:5), a short retelling of their whole story. Chapters 27–28 then set out the blessings and curses of the covenant.

Deuteronomy 27.summary: Moses and the elders tell Israel that when they cross the Jordan, they are to set up large stones, coat them with plaster, and write all the words of the law on them (Deuteronomy 27:1-4). They are also to build an altar of uncut stones on Mount Ebal, offer burnt and peace offerings, and rejoice before the LORD (Deuteronomy 27:5-8). Moses and the Levitical priests remind Israel that they are now the people of the LORD (Deuteronomy 27:9-10). Six tribes (Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Joseph, and Benjamin) are to stand on Mount Gerizim to bless, and six (Reuben, Gad, Asher, Zebulun, Dan, and Naphtali) on Mount Ebal to curse (Deuteronomy 27:11-13). The Levites then pronounce twelve curses on secret idolatry, dishonoring parents, moving boundary markers, mistreating the vulnerable, various sexual sins, secret murder, taking bribes, and failing to uphold the law, and all the people respond 'Amen' (Deuteronomy 27:14-26).
Deuteronomy 27.whereWeAre: The laws of chapters 12–26 are finished. Now Moses tells Israel to write them on stones once they cross the Jordan and to hold a ceremony of blessing and cursing at Mount Gerizim and Mount Ebal. Joshua carries this out in Joshua 8, and chapter 28 spells out the blessings and curses in full.

Deuteronomy 28.summary: This chapter lays out the consequences of obeying or disobeying the covenant. If Israel carefully obeys, the LORD will set them high above all nations and bless them in the city and field, in family and livestock, in coming and going, in storehouses, and in defeat of enemies (Deuteronomy 28:1-14). If they do not, a long list of curses will overtake them: disease, drought, crop failure, defeat, oppression, madness, and loss of family and land (Deuteronomy 28:15-46). Because they did not serve the LORD joyfully, a distant nation will besiege them to the point of horrific famine (Deuteronomy 28:47-57). The curses include a return to the plagues of Egypt, scattering among the nations, anxiety, and a possible return to slavery in Egypt (Deuteronomy 28:58-68).
Deuteronomy 28.whereWeAre: Chapter 27 set up a ceremony of blessing and cursing. This chapter spells out what obedience and disobedience will bring, ending with the warning of exile. Much of Israel's later history, all the way to Babylon, reads like these curses coming true, and chapters 29–30 call Israel to renew the covenant.

Deuteronomy 29.summary: Moses renews the covenant on the plains of Moab, in addition to the covenant at Horeb (Deuteronomy 29:1). He summons all Israel and recalls what they saw in Egypt and in the wilderness: the LORD provided for them for forty years, defeated Sihon and Og, and gave their land to the Transjordan tribes (Deuteronomy 29:2-8). Everyone is present, from leaders to children, wives, and foreigners who chop wood and draw water, to enter this covenant today, along with generations not yet born (Deuteronomy 29:10-15). Moses warns against anyone secretly turning to other gods, "a root that beareth gall and wormwood" (Deuteronomy 29:16-21). Future generations and foreigners will ask why the land is devastated, and the answer will be that Israel abandoned the covenant (Deuteronomy 29:22-28). The chapter ends: "The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever" (Deuteronomy 29:29).
Deuteronomy 29.whereWeAre: Moses has finished the laws and the blessings and curses of chapters 12–28. Now he calls the whole nation, from leaders to children, to renew the covenant on the plains of Moab. Chapter 30 finishes his appeal with a call to choose.

Deuteronomy 30.summary: Moses anticipates that after Israel experiences the blessings and curses and is scattered among the nations, they may come to their senses. If they return to the LORD with all their heart and soul and obey him, the LORD will restore their fortunes, gather them from the nations, and bring them back to the land (Deuteronomy 30:1-5). The LORD will circumcise their hearts so they love him (Deuteronomy 30:6) and will turn the curses on their enemies (Deuteronomy 30:7). The commandment, Moses says, is not too hard or far away; it is very near, in their mouth and heart (Deuteronomy 30:11-14). He sets before them life and good, death and evil, and calls on heaven and earth as witnesses. "therefore choose life, that both thou and thy seed may live" (Deuteronomy 30:15-20).
Deuteronomy 30.whereWeAre: Moses warned in chapters 28–29 that disobedience will lead to exile. This chapter looks past that to hope: even scattered Israel can return to God. It ends with Moses' final appeal, "therefore choose life" (Deuteronomy 30:19), and chapter 31 begins his last days.

Deuteronomy 31.summary: Moses, now 120 years old, tells Israel he can no longer lead and will not cross the Jordan; the LORD will go before them, and Joshua will lead (Deuteronomy 31:1-6). He charges Joshua before all Israel, "Be strong and of a good courage," for the LORD will not fail or forsake him (Deuteronomy 31:7-8). Moses writes down the law and gives it to the priests and elders, commanding that it be read publicly to all Israel every seven years at the Feast of Booths, including men, women, children, and foreigners (Deuteronomy 31:9-13). The LORD summons Moses and Joshua to the tent of meeting, predicts that Israel will turn to other gods, and commissions a song to serve as a witness (Deuteronomy 31:14-22). Joshua is commissioned (Deuteronomy 31:23). The book of the law is placed beside the ark as a witness against the people's stubbornness (Deuteronomy 31:24-29), and Moses recites the song (Deuteronomy 31:30).
Deuteronomy 31.whereWeAre: Moses has finished his speeches in chapters 1–30. Now, at 120 years old, he hands leadership to Joshua, writes down the law, and is told that Israel will turn away after he dies. He teaches them a song as a witness, which chapter 32 records.

Deuteronomy 32.summary: Moses recites the Song of Moses. He calls heaven and earth to listen and praises the LORD as the Rock whose work is perfect and whose ways are just (Deuteronomy 32:1-4). Israel, however, acted corruptly, forgetting the Father who made them (Deuteronomy 32:5-6). The song recalls how God found Israel in the wilderness, cared for them as an eagle "beareth them on her wings," and gave them the land (Deuteronomy 32:7-14). Jeshurun grew fat and rebelled, sacrificing to other gods (Deuteronomy 32:15-18). The LORD responds with anger and judgment, but refuses to let the nations claim credit and promises to vindicate his people and have compassion on his servants (Deuteronomy 32:19-43). Moses then urges the people to take these words to heart (Deuteronomy 32:44-47). Finally, the LORD tells Moses to go up Mount Nebo, view the land, and die there, because he broke faith with the LORD at Meribath-kadesh (Deuteronomy 32:48-52).
Deuteronomy 32.whereWeAre: God told Moses in chapter 31 to teach Israel a song. This chapter is that song, retelling God's faithfulness and Israel's unfaithfulness. Afterward God tells Moses to climb Mount Nebo to see the land and die, and chapter 33 records his final blessing.

Deuteronomy 33.summary: Before his death, Moses blesses the tribes of Israel. He begins by describing the LORD coming from Sinai, Seir, and Paran with holy ones at his right hand, loving his people (Deuteronomy 33:1-5). The blessings that follow address Reuben, Judah, Levi (with the Urim and Thummim, and teaching and sacrificing roles), Benjamin, Joseph, Zebulun and Issachar, Gad, Dan, Naphtali, and Asher (Deuteronomy 33:6-25). Simeon is not mentioned. The final section praises the LORD as incomparable, a refuge with everlasting arms, and declares Israel secure and blessed: "Happy art thou, O Israel: who is like unto thee, O people saved by the LORD" (Deuteronomy 33:26-29).
Deuteronomy 33.whereWeAre: God has just told Moses in chapter 32 that he will die on Mount Nebo. Before he goes, Moses blesses each tribe, much as Jacob blessed his sons in Genesis 49. His last words are full of hope, "underneath are the everlasting arms" (Deuteronomy 33:27), and chapter 34 tells of his death.

Deuteronomy 34.summary: Moses climbs from the plains of Moab up Mount Nebo to the top of Pisgah opposite Jericho, and the LORD shows him the land from Gilead to Dan, all of Naphtali, Ephraim and Manasseh, Judah as far as the western sea, the Negeb, and the plain of Jericho. The LORD says, "I have caused thee to see it with thine eyes, but thou shalt not go over thither" (Deuteronomy 34:1-4). Moses dies there at the LORD's command, and the LORD buries him in a valley in Moab; "no man knoweth of his sepulchre unto this day" (Deuteronomy 34:5-6). He was 120, and "his eye was not dim, nor his natural force abated" (Deuteronomy 34:7). Israel mourns for thirty days (Deuteronomy 34:8). Joshua, filled with the spirit of wisdom, takes over leadership (Deuteronomy 34:9). The book closes by saying that no prophet like Moses has arisen in Israel, who knew the LORD face to face and did signs and wonders in Egypt (Deuteronomy 34:10-12).
Deuteronomy 34.whereWeAre: Moses gave his last blessing in chapter 33. Now he climbs Mount Nebo, sees the promised land, and dies. This ends the first five books of the Bible, and the story continues in Joshua as Israel finally crosses the Jordan.
